title: To become UN Secretary-General you need 9 of 15 Council votes, and not a single veto
body: The UN Charter says the General Assembly appoints the Secretary-General on the recommendation of the Security Council, which needs nine of its 15 votes and no veto from its five permanent members: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Before the formal vote, the Council tests each candidate in secret straw polls, voting to encourage, discourage or express no opinion. On 16 October 2026 the sixth poll for a successor to António Guterres, whose second term ends on 31 December, was the first this year to give the permanent members red ballots. Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica led with nine encourages, but [AP reported](https://abcnews.com/US/wireStory/latest-vote-shows-candidate-chief-required-support-key-137340089) that she and the two runners-up each drew two red discourages, a sign of a possible veto, so no candidate yet has the support of all five. In 2016 the first red-ballot poll showed Guterres with 13 encourages and no discourage, and the Council recommended him the next day.

slides.question: In 2016’s first red-ballot straw poll, how many of the 15 Security Council members encouraged António Guterres?
slides.explanation: 13, with no discourage at all and two no opinions. The Council recommended him by acclamation the next day, and the General Assembly appointed him a week later.

slides.alt: Animation on deep blue with the UN emblem’s polar grid: the Security Council as a horseshoe of 15 seats, five of them red, and ballot cards marked encourage, discourage or no opinion. Rows of white ballots turn red for the permanent members on 16 October; then the 2016 poll that chose Guterres.

slides.prompt: These are Rebeca Grynspan’s 15 ballots from 16 October. Tap ballots to change them, and get her through with as few changes as you can.
slides.takeaway: Two changes are enough: the two red discourages. She already had nine encourages, and no number of white ballots could outweigh a single red one.

The first secret straw poll in the Council.
The sixth poll, the first with red ballots.

slides.heading: What a red ballot means
slides.text: A red discourage is not yet a veto: straw polls are informal, and positions can change before the formal vote. But it warns a candidate that a permanent member may block them. Without colours, a candidate could not tell whether a discourage came from one of the five or from an elected member.

slides.question: In a straw poll for Secretary-General, what can a Council member mark on each candidate’s ballot?
slides.explanation: Members encourage or discourage each candidate, or express no opinion. Since 16 October 2026 the five permanent members vote on red ballots.
